description:
We’re building a health monitoring application for astronauts, focusing on usability, meaningful health insights, and effective decision support.

I'm a product designer, and I'll be contributing to product strategy, UX, UI, and AI-assisted development.

Looking for teammates with experience or interest in software development, data science, biomedical engineering, human physiology, NASA datasets, data visualization, or health monitoring systems.

All experience levels are welcome.
summary: HAOMA is a web prototype that helps astronauts check the six health indicators named in the challenge: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, and mood. Each reading is checked against evidence-labeled rules and the astronaut's own baseline, then shown as Normal, Attention, or Escalate, with what to do first. In space, early signs are easy to miss and care is far away. HAOMA makes self-assessment quick, consistent, and honest about its limits.
details:
What it does and how it works

Daily check-in

"Log reading" opens one dialog with a tab per indicator, so an astronaut can log one or more readings at once. The app records the context that changes what a number means: at rest or after activity, fasting or not, oral or forehead thermometer, and how sleep was measured.

Evaluation

Each reading is checked against evidence-labeled rules approved by the team. Every rule carries its sources and an evidence label: Spaceflight evidence, General clinical reference, Team design decision, or Simulated demo logic. After five readings, the app compares new readings with the astronaut's personal baseline (the median of the last seven). A reading that no rule covers is shown as "Not evaluated", never as Normal.

Guidance

Each result says what to do first, for example "Re-measure after rest and watch the trend" or "Tell the flight surgeon at your next contact". A "Why?" section shows the rule, its source, and the type of evidence. The mission phase (in flight, approaching landing, post-landing) adds landing-specific reminders.

History and context

Each indicator has a chart and a table that can be edited and paged. A 3D/2D body map records self-reported pain and saves it as a report for the flight surgeon; it is never interpreted. An optional crew comparison shows the average of the other crew members on the same mission day, comparing like with like, as context only. It never changes a status.

Benefits and intended impact

On long missions, care is far away and communication is delayed. HAOMA aims to make daily self-assessment take minutes, to apply the same rules every time, and to make it clear when to involve the flight surgeon. Every result can be traced to its source, so astronauts and medical teams can see why the app said what it said.

Tools

React and TypeScript with Vite, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui (Radix), Lucide icons, and Recharts. The body map uses a small WebGL and SVG engine without extra libraries. Tested with Vitest and Testing Library (340 automated tests), checked with oxlint and Prettier, hosted on Vercel, code on GitHub. Designed and developed with VS Code, and FigJam. Development was assisted by Claude Code, the Claude app, and ChatGPT (SI), as disclosed in the repository.

What makes it creative

Every rule shows its evidence, so the app is open about what is and isn't known for astronauts. The interface theme can follow the mission zone (Earth, Space, Moon, Mars). The body map lets astronauts point to where it hurts instead of describing it. The crew comparison gives mission context while protecting privacy.

Factors we considered

Safety

The app never diagnoses, and urgent results name who to contact and when.

Evidence

General-population ranges are labeled as not validated for astronauts.

Measurement context

Readings taken in different ways are kept apart, for example oral and forehead temperatures, or resting and after-activity heart rates.

Privacy

Data stays in the browser, and the crew comparison shows only averages from at least three people.

Accessibility

High contrast, text size, assistive patterns so status never depends on colour, keyboard use, and screen-reader labels.

Honesty

The astronaut, crew, and demo data are fictional and labeled as simulated.

Live app: https://haomaho.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/shahyari/haoma
